items.title: Jack DeJohnette — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: Did some trio gigs with McCoy.

ctx.x: Well yeah, he came later. That was my first band that toured internationally. We started touring Europe, and George was getting gigs on the fly as we were going over there and getting a lot of press. He knew how to bill the band. We were constantly going to Europe and then coming back, then going out to the West coast. That group subsequently got invited in ‘67… …we got invited to play in Russia and we got invited there, no fee, no money, but George saw this as great exposure, for the band to get international…

we got there they had to hide us. There was a knock on the door and they were asking "Was anybody there?" and they said "No no, there's nobody there," and we don't know what happened to this guy after we left, but George capitalized on it and we got a lot of press from that. . . When we came back, the Dreamweaver album apparently sold over a million copies, which for that time was really good. The Charles Lloyd Quartet was bridging that crossover stuff that was happening, and then we played gigs opposite Miles…
So we left off talking about your trip in 1966 back to Chicago to perform with John Coltrane and Alice and Pharaoh...

items.title: Jack DeJohnette interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, April 7, 2025
items.q: it’s McCoy Tyner, it was McCoy’s gig, McCoy Tyner, Joey Henderson, Henry Grimes and myself.

ctx.x: As time goes by I’ve spoken to musicians about searching for their own original sound or being creative, and I wonder if it gets harder as people come and go and they make their contributions and you’re trying to find something that hasn’t been done before. Does it get harder as the years go by?

Well not if you, you know assess the terrain, what’s going on. The most important thing is to find your own voice and just be real with that, and then go from there. And not be in competition, just being yourself. Having something that the music produces and fans can connect to. There’s one more album I’d like to say, it wasn’t my album but we have archive recordings here, and this is a recording from 1966 at the legendary club Slug’s and it’s McCoy Tyner, it was McCoy’s gig, McCoy Tyner, Joey Henderson, Henry…

items.title: Tyner McCoy — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: So on this album Inner Voices, some tracks have Eric Gravatt, some tracks have Jack DeJohnette.

ctx.x: together; and Hubert could play any kind of music, you could play symphonic music, a lot of different stuff.

So on this album Inner Voices, some tracks have Eric Gravatt, some tracks have Jack DeJohnette. Now we’ve talked about Jack, and he’s going to keep coming back up because he keeps coming back into the fold, just like Elvin, and Eric Gravatt comes back. So you had this special relationship with drummers. I guess because on the piano that left hand is another drum.
I had to fire the left hand because it was dominating (laughs). I’m sorry, but I like to laugh. He’s a good guy.
